cards.name: Delivery spec: YouTube upload (16:9, HD and 4K)
cards.summary: What to export for YouTube, per YouTube's own recommended upload settings: MP4, H.264 High profile, progressive, closed GOP of half the frame rate, 4:2:0, BT.709, AAC-LC 48 kHz; SDR bitrates 8 Mbps (1080p 24/25/30), 12 Mbps (1080p 48/50/60), 35-45 Mbps (2160p 24/25/30), 53-68 Mbps (2160p 48/50/60); stereo audio 384 kbps.
use_for: long-form explainers and documentaries on YouTube
picking the .epr the pipeline exports with
QC of a file before upload
cards.how: Premiere H.264, starting from a 'Match Source - High bitrate' style preset: Profile High; Field Order Progressive; frame rate = the sequence's (do not convert at export); Bitrate Encoding VBR 2-pass, Target Bitrate from YouTube's table (8 / 12 / 35-45 / 53-68 Mbps); Key Frame Distance = half the frame rate (15 at 30 fps) where the encoder exposes it; Audio AAC, 48 kHz, Stereo, 384 kbps; Export Color Space Rec. 709. Working defaults beyond YouTube's table: target 1.5-2x the table for grainy or text-heavy pictures (YouTube re-encodes everything, so a heavier upload only costs upload time), max bitrate about 1.5x target, and the loudness target from 'Delivery loudness targets'. Premiere: File > Export > Media (or the Export mode), Format + Preset, then the Video / Audio tabs; save the result as an .epr preset so scripts can reuse it (Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect(out, epr, workArea) or app.encoder.encodeSequence(...) to Media Encoder; PVE Export and Media Encoder cards). Verify every file: ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_name,profile,width,height,r_frame_rate,field_order,bit_rate,color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space,sample_rate,channels -of compact <file>.
cards.script_api: Export through a saved .epr: Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect(outPath, eprPath, app.encoder.ENCODE_ENTIRE) or app.encoder.encodeSequence(seq, outPath, eprPath, workArea, removeOnCompletion); UXP EncoderManager.exportSequence. The .epr is XML: write one per destination and keep it in the repo's own presets, never a copied Adobe file.
cards.limits: YouTube lists 'recommended' settings, not limits; it also accepts other codecs (and Opus / Eclipsa audio). Two consecutive B-frames and the GOP are not exposed by every Premiere H.264 encoder (hardware encoding is limited to CBR and VBR 1-pass, per Adobe's best-practice notes seen only in search results). HDR uploads have their own table on the same page.

cards.name: Delivery spec: vertical Reels, Shorts and TikTok (9:16)
cards.summary: What to export for vertical platforms: 9:16, progressive, fixed frame rate, square pixels, H.264 MP4 (or MOV), stereo AAC. Meta's Reels ads guide recommends 1440x2560, up to 15 min and 4 GB, AAC 128 kbps or more, and keeping 14% top, 35% bottom and 6% each side free of text and logos. TikTok's ad pages ask for 540x960 or larger; YouTube has no published Shorts encode or safe-zone spec.
use_for: Instagram / Facebook Reels, YouTube Shorts and TikTok deliveries
one master export for all three
QC before posting
cards.how: Working default (one file for all three): 1080x1920 (or 1440x2560 for Meta ads), the sequence's frame rate (25 or 30, constant), H.264 High, VBR 2-pass target 12-16 Mbps / max 20 (working default: the platforms re-encode, so this is headroom, not a requirement), AAC 48 kHz stereo 320 kbps (Meta's floor is 128), Rec.709. Keep text and faces inside the UI-free area: 'Platform UI safe zones (1080x1920)'. Premiere: File > Export > Media (or the Export mode), Format + Preset, then the Video / Audio tabs; save the result as an .epr preset so scripts can reuse it (Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect(out, epr, workArea) or app.encoder.encodeSequence(...) to Media Encoder; PVE Export and Media Encoder cards). Verify every file: ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_name,profile,width,height,r_frame_rate,field_order,bit_rate,color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space,sample_rate,channels -of compact <file>.
cards.script_api: As for YouTube: a saved .epr per destination + Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect / app.encoder.encodeSequence; Auto Reframe (Sequence.autoReframeSequence) to make the 9:16 sequence from a 16:9 edit (PVE Auto Reframe card).
cards.limits: Instagram's organic upload spec page could not be read (it returned no content), so organic numbers are the ads guide's. TikTok's pages were read only through search snippets (its 'Bitrate: More than or equal to 516 kbps' has an unclear unit); no TikTok codec requirement was found. Shorts: no official Google spec found. Meta gives the safe zone in percent, not pixels.

cards.name: Delivery spec: broadcast masters (ProRes 422 HQ, XDCAM HD422 MXF OP1a)
cards.summary: The two common HD broadcast file masters: Apple ProRes 422 HQ in .mov (1920x1080 target 184 Mb/s at 25p, 220 Mb/s at 29.97p) and XDCAM HD422 (MPEG-2 4:2:2P@HL, 50 Mb/s CBR) in MXF OP1a, with 24-bit 48 kHz PCM audio. The broadcaster's spec sheet always wins: field order, track layout, loudness, slate and timecode come from it.
use_for: TV news and documentary deliveries
handing a programme to a channel's playout
choosing between a ProRes and an MXF deliverable
cards.how: Premiere / Media Encoder: Format QuickTime > Video Codec Apple ProRes 422 HQ (frame size and rate = sequence, Render at Maximum Depth on for graded or graphics-heavy edits), audio Uncompressed 48 kHz 24-bit; or Format MXF OP1a > an XDCAM HD 50 preset (Media Encoder lists 'XDCAMHD 50' under MXF OP1a, and AS-10 variants). Field Order: as the channel specifies (interlaced 1080i deliveries need an interlaced sequence or a deliberate conversion; never let the export guess). Audio channel layout and loudness: 'Broadcast audio track layouts (EBU R 123)' and 'Delivery loudness targets'. Premiere: File > Export > Media (or the Export mode), Format + Preset, then the Video / Audio tabs; save the result as an .epr preset so scripts can reuse it (Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect(out, epr, workArea) or app.encoder.encodeSequence(...) to Media Encoder; PVE Export and Media Encoder cards). Verify every file: ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_name,profile,width,height,r_frame_rate,field_order,bit_rate,color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space,sample_rate,channels -of compact <file>.
cards.script_api: Same export calls with a saved ProRes or MXF .epr; Media Encoder presets are per-machine files, so the pipeline should ship its own .epr rather than reference an installed preset path.
cards.limits: ProRes data rates are Apple's targets (actual rates vary with content). The MXF OP1a wrapper for XDCAM HD422 is stated by Autodesk's format list and implied by Adobe's export table; Sony's camera page gives the codec and 50 Mb/s but not 'OP1a'. Adobe notes some formats are only available depending on the installed apps (seen in search results only). UK-style AS-11 / DPP files have their own metadata rules not covered here.

cards.name: Delivery spec: mezzanine and archive masters
cards.summary: What to keep after delivery: a high-quality mezzanine (ProRes 422 HQ, or 4444 / 4444 XQ for graphics-heavy or keyed work) from which every platform file can be re-made, plus the project, its collected media and the audio stems. Apple's 1920x1080 targets at 29.97: 422 HQ 220, 4444 330, 4444 XQ 495 Mb/s (25p: 184, 275, 413).
use_for: re-exporting for a new platform without re-rendering effects
archive of finished programmes
handing a master to a colourist or another editor
cards.how: Working default: master = ProRes 422 HQ at the sequence's size and rate, Rec.709 tagged, stereo (or the programme's channel layout) 48 kHz 24-bit PCM; graphics or keyed composites = ProRes 4444; archive folder = master .mov + stems (dialogue / music / effects WAVs: 'Stems and split-track export') + the project collected with Project Manager / Collect Files ('Collect a project for hand-off') + fonts list. Make platform files FROM the master, not from the timeline, when the timeline is slow to render. Premiere: File > Export > Media (or the Export mode), Format + Preset, then the Video / Audio tabs; save the result as an .epr preset so scripts can reuse it (Sequence.exportAsMediaDirect(out, epr, workArea) or app.encoder.encodeSequence(...) to Media Encoder; PVE Export and Media Encoder cards). Verify every file: ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_name,profile,width,height,r_frame_rate,field_order,bit_rate,color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space,sample_rate,channels -of compact <file>.
cards.script_api: Export the master with a ProRes .epr; transcode platform files with Media Encoder (app.encoder.encodeFile(in, out, epr, ...)) or ffmpeg.
cards.limits: Codec choice for archives is a working default (ProRes is an Apple codec; DNxHR HQX is the common Avid alternative, rates not checked here). ProRes 4444 numbers are labelled 'no alpha' in Apple's table: alpha adds to them.

cards.name: Delivery spec: alpha overlays (ProRes 4444, PNG sequence)
cards.summary: How to deliver graphics with transparency (lower thirds, tickers, logos, keyed elements) for compositing in another edit: ProRes 4444 or 4444 XQ .mov (the only ProRes flavours that carry alpha) or a PNG sequence (RGB + alpha, lossless). H.264 and HEVC .mp4 deliveries have no usable alpha.
use_for: overlay packs for other editors (ticker, straps, bugs)
AE graphics into a Premiere edit without Dynamic Link
sending keyed plates to a compositor
cards.how: After Effects: Render Queue > Output Module: QuickTime, Apple ProRes 4444, Channels RGB + Alpha (vfx.py uses the 'High Quality with Alpha' template for scenes with 'alpha': true); or PNG Sequence, RGB + Alpha. Choose Straight or Premultiplied colour deliberately and tell the receiver (straight is the safer hand-off; premultiplied against black shows dark fringes if interpreted as straight). Premiere: export Apple ProRes 4444 with alpha (the Video tab's alpha / depth option). Check: ffprobe pix_fmt shows yuva444p10le (ProRes 4444 with alpha) or rgba (PNG).
cards.script_api: AE: OutputModule.applyTemplate('High Quality with Alpha') or setSettings; Premiere: an .epr with alpha enabled
cards.limits: The codec inside AE's 'High Quality with Alpha' template was not read back on this install. A PNG sequence is large and needs frame-rate interpretation on import. Premiere's exact alpha checkbox label in 26.x was not verified.

cards.name: Export encoding choices: VBR 2-pass vs CBR, maximum depth and quality, field order
cards.summary: The export switches that matter beyond the preset: bitrate mode (CBR faster, VBR better quality per size, 2-pass more efficient than 1-pass), Render at Maximum Depth (renders at the format's highest bit depth, usually 32-bit float), Use Maximum Render Quality (helps when scaling to a different frame size), and Field Order (progressive vs interlaced fields).
use_for: choosing between fast drafts and final masters
avoiding banding on gradients and graphics
exports that change frame size (4K source to HD, 16:9 to 9:16)
cards.how: Drafts: VBR 1-pass (or hardware encoding). Finals for the web: VBR 2-pass at the destination's target bitrate ('Delivery spec' cards). Broadcast: the channel's mode (XDCAM HD422 is CBR). Turn on Render at Maximum Depth for graded, gradient-heavy or 10-bit sources, and Use Maximum Render Quality when the export size differs from the sequence or sources were scaled. Field Order: Progressive for every web destination.
cards.script_api: All of these are fields inside the .epr (XML): set them once in Premiere, save the preset, and export with it from scripts.
cards.limits: Adobe's wording: VBR 2-pass 'lengthens encoding times but ensures greater encoding efficiency' (export settings page). Hardware encoders are limited to CBR and VBR 1-pass (Adobe best-practice page, seen only in search results).

cards.name: Colour tags on export: Rec.709 colr/nclc and the QuickTime gamma shift
cards.summary: Why an H.264 export can look washed out or brighter on a Mac (QuickTime, Safari, some phone apps) but fine in Premiere: the file is tagged BT.709 (QuickTime 'colr' atom 'nclc' 1-1-1 / H.264 VUI 1-1-1) and macOS displays it at about gamma 1.96, Windows about 2.2, while Premiere's viewer works at broadcast 2.4. Adobe's fix is awareness and a viewer setting, not a different export.
use_for: answering 'my export looks washed out'
checking that exports carry Rec.709 tags
repairing an untagged file without re-encoding
cards.how: Premiere: Lumetri Color > Settings > Project > Viewer Gamma: '2.4 (Broadcast)', '2.2 (Web)' or '1.96 (QuickTime)' to preview how a destination will show it (Adobe: changing Viewer Gamma does not change the export). Export Color Space defaults to Rec. 709 for most presets: leave it. Check the tags: ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=color_primaries,color_transfer,color_space,color_range -of compact <file> -> bt709 / bt709 / bt709 / tv. Repair an untagged H.264 without re-encoding: ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -bsf:v h264_metadata=colour_primaries=1:transfer_characteristics=1:matrix_coefficients=1 out.mp4. When re-encoding with ffmpeg: -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 (and -color_range tv).
cards.script_api: No scripting API for Viewer Gamma; tags are set by the export preset (.epr) or fixed afterwards with ffmpeg.
cards.limits: Gamma values per OS are Adobe's statement; how each phone app or browser displays tagged video varies and was not measured here. The mov muxer's -movflags write_colr is documented as experimental (may be renamed, not for scripts). Viewer Gamma needs Color Setup 'Direct Rec. 709 (SDR)' or colour management disabled (search-result summary, not read on the page). Full vs legal range errors are a different problem: 'Full vs legal range fix'.

cards.name: Photosensitive flash rule (Harding / ITU-R BT.1702) and pve check
cards.summary: The photosensitive epilepsy rule every delivery must meet: no more than 3 flashes in any one second where the flashing covers more than a quarter of the screen (ITU-R BT.1702-3, Ofcom). A flash is a pair of opposing brightness changes of 20 cd/m2 or more where the darker image is below 160 cd/m2; any change to or from saturated red counts; regular stripe patterns are covered too. pve.check_spec and check_scenes enforce the 3-per-second limit.
use_for: any edit with strobes, flash transitions, flicker or fast cuts between bright and dark
music videos and hype reels
QC before a broadcast or ad delivery
cards.how: Numbers (BT.1702-3 / Ofcom): flashes are acceptable when their leading edges are at least 360 ms apart at 50 Hz (9 frames at 25 fps) or 334 ms at 60 Hz; more than 5 light-dark stripe pairs is a harmful pattern when stationary over more than 40% of the screen or moving over more than 25%; flashing that lasts more than 5 s can be risky even when it complies. Web (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.3.1): a flash is a change of 10% or more of relative luminance with the darker image below 0.80, over more than a 341x256 px area at 1024x768. In PVE: cards that flash carry a 'flash' field (per_frame, period, rate, per_use, quiet, basis); pve.check_spec / check_scenes rate every such effect, preset and transition from the spec's own values and report more than pve.FLASH_LIMIT (3) flashes a second as an issue; where no rate can be computed the line starts 'check by eye' and is advisory. UK broadcast and advertising deliveries are commonly checked with a Harding FPA test (the ASA asks ads to pass one or an equivalent).
cards.script_api: pve.check_spec(spec) / pve.check_scenes(scenes) -> issue lines (flash lines included); pve.FLASH_LIMIT = 3; pve.advisory(line) is true for 'check by eye' lines. Measuring a render: per-frame mean luma (ffmpeg signalstats) is a rough screen, not a BT.1702 analyser.
cards.limits: PVE counts flashes per effect or transition from card data; it does not analyse rendered pixels, does not add a strobe clip to a nearby flash transition (pve.py notes this), and cannot judge red flashes or patterns: the final render still needs a proper analyser (Harding FPA or equivalent) for broadcast. Ofcom's guidance cites Harding's research but does not itself require the Harding test.
